cards.front: A cell's jobs, from a muscle pulling to building proteins, run on {{c1::ATP}}, not on glucose directly.
cards.quote: from a muscle pulling to a nerve cell pumping charged particles to building proteins, run on ATP, not on glucose directly
cards.section: Explain: ATP carries energy to where it is used

cards.front: About how many ATP does one glucose rebuild when it is taken all the way down with oxygen, and how many when it stops partway at lactate or ethanol?
cards.back: About 30 ATP with oxygen; only 2 when it stops partway.
cards.quote: A glucose taken all the way down to carbon dioxide and water, with oxygen, rebuilds about 30 ATP.
cards.section: Explain: ATP carries energy to where it is used

cards.front: Breaking any chemical bond takes energy. So how can ATP release energy when its end phosphate comes off?
cards.back: The energy comes from the whole reaction, not one bond. The products, ADP and phosphate, are more stable (lower in energy) than ATP and water were. The difference is usable energy.
cards.quote: The products, ADP and phosphate, end up more stable than ATP and water were, meaning lower in energy.
cards.section: Explain: ATP carries energy to where it is used

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say that ATP is energy?
cards.back: ATP is a molecule. It releases usable energy when it loses a phosphate, really changing into ADP and a loose phosphate, and is then rebuilt.
cards.quote: Unlike a battery, though, ATP really changes into ADP and a loose phosphate, and is then rebuilt.
cards.section: Explain: ATP carries energy to where it is used

cards.front: A working cell keeps turning ATP into ADP and phosphate. What role does respiration play in keeping its ATP supply going?
cards.back: Respiration supplies the energy to add a phosphate back onto ADP, rebuilding ATP. ATP and ADP go round in a cycle.
cards.quote: respiration supplies the energy to add the phosphate back
cards.section: Explain: ATP carries energy to where it is used

cards.front: A muscle cell is full of glucose, but all its ATP has been turned into ADP and none can be rebuilt. Can the muscle still pull? Why?
cards.back: No. Muscle work runs on ATP, not on glucose directly. The glucose's energy is useless to the muscle unless it is used to rebuild ATP from ADP.
cards.why: Rule: a cell's jobs run on ATP; the cell rebuilds ATP from ADP with energy from taking glucose apart.
cards.quote: The cell rebuilds ATP from ADP with energy from taking glucose apart.
cards.section: Explain: ATP carries energy to where it is used

cards.front: {{c1::Cellular respiration}} is cells breaking down glucose and other food molecules and using the released energy to build ATP.
cards.back: It happens in plants, animals, fungi and many microbes.
cards.quote: Cellular respiration is cells breaking down glucose and other food molecules and using the released energy to build ATP, in plants, animals, fungi and many microbes.
cards.section: Explain: where ATP is rebuilt

cards.front: Respiration equation: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → {{c1::6CO2 + 6H2O}} + energy (much of it captured in ATP)
cards.back: Glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water.
cards.quote: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (much of it captured in ATP)
cards.section: Explain: where ATP is rebuilt

cards.front: In C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O, count the carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms on each side. What does the count show?
cards.back: Left: 6 C, 12 H, 6 + 12 = 18 O. Right: 6 C (6CO2), 12 H (6H2O), 12 + 6 = 18 O. The atoms match, so matter is rearranged, not created or lost.
cards.quote: Check the atoms: 6 carbons, 12 hydrogens and 18 oxygens on each side.
cards.section: Explain: where ATP is rebuilt

cards.front: In a cell with oxygen, where does respiration start, and where is most of the ATP made?
cards.back: It starts in the cytoplasm; most ATP is made in the mitochondria.
cards.quote: Starts in the cytoplasm; most ATP made in mitochondria
cards.section: Explain: with oxygen and without it

cards.front: When glucose is broken down in respiration, where does its energy go?
cards.back: Into ATP and into heat, which warms you when you exercise. No energy is made or destroyed.
cards.quote: No energy is made or destroyed: it moves from glucose into ATP and heat.
cards.section: Explain: where ATP is rebuilt

cards.front: Aerobic means using oxygen; {{c1::anaerobic}} means without it.
cards.quote: Aerobic means using oxygen; anaerobic means without it.
cards.section: Explain: with oxygen and without it

cards.front: Biologists call this route {{c1::fermentation}}: making a small amount of ATP from glucose without oxygen.
cards.quote: Biologists call this route fermentation: making a small amount of ATP from glucose without oxygen.
cards.section: Explain: with oxygen and without it

cards.front: What does fermentation make in a muscle cell, and what does it make in yeast?
cards.back: Muscle: lactate. Yeast: ethanol and carbon dioxide.
cards.quote: Muscle: lactate. Yeast: ethanol and carbon dioxide
cards.section: Explain: with oxygen and without it

cards.front: The SOL calls fermentation "anaerobic respiration." Why can that name be confusing?
cards.back: Biologists also use "anaerobic respiration" for something different that some microbes do: using another substance, such as nitrate or sulfate, in place of oxygen.
cards.quote: The SOL calls it anaerobic respiration, a name biologists also use for something different that some microbes do
cards.section: Explain: with oxygen and without it

cards.front: Turning glucose halves into lactate or ethanol adds no ATP. Why does a cell bother with that last step?
cards.back: The first steps, which make the 2 ATP, use up a small helper molecule (NAD+). Making lactate or ethanol hands the helper back, so the first steps can keep running.
cards.quote: Turning the halves into lactate or ethanol hands that helper back, so the first steps can keep running.
cards.section: Explain: with oxygen and without it

cards.front: In a sprinting leg, do the mitochondria stop when lactate starts to form?
cards.back: No. It is not all or nothing. The mitochondria keep working; lactate forms when the first steps make halves faster than the mitochondria can take them in.
cards.quote: A sprinting leg can need ATP faster than that route supplies it, even with its mitochondria working
cards.section: Explain: where ATP is rebuilt

cards.front: Lactate still holds most of glucose's energy. Does the body throw it away as waste?
cards.back: No. The heart, other muscles and the liver use lactate as fuel or to rebuild glucose.
cards.quote: the heart, other muscles and the liver use it as fuel or to rebuild glucose.
cards.section: Explain: with oxygen and without it

cards.front: Is the burn in your legs during a sprint caused by lactate? What about soreness the next day?
cards.back: The burn is not from lactate alone; experiments point to a mix of acid, lactate and other chemicals. Next-day soreness is a different effect, and lactate is not its cause.
cards.quote: The burn is not caused by lactate alone; experiments point to a mix of acid, lactate and other chemicals.
cards.section: Explain: with oxygen and without it

cards.front: Using classroom values (about 30 ATP per glucose with oxygen, 2 by fermentation), how many glucose molecules does a cell need for 90 ATP with oxygen, and how many without?
cards.back: With oxygen: 90 ÷ 30 = 3 glucose. Without oxygen: 90 ÷ 2 = 45 glucose.
cards.quote: Key idea: A glucose taken all the way down with oxygen gives about 30 ATP
cards.section: Explain: with oxygen and without it

cards.front: In the virtual cell, oxygen is off and the glucose supply doubles. Predict what happens to ATP made per glucose and ATP made per second.
cards.back: ATP per glucose stays at 2, because the route is still fermentation. ATP per second rises, because more glucose is broken down each second.
cards.why: Rule: how far glucose is taken apart sets the ATP per glucose; the supply only changes how fast ATP is made.
cards.quote: Keep oxygen off and double the glucose supply.
cards.section: Explore: run a cell’s energy budget

cards.front: A sprinter's leg needs ATP faster than aerobic respiration alone can supply it, even with the mitochondria working. What happens, and what builds up?
cards.back: Fermentation adds quick ATP, and lactate builds up in the muscle.
cards.why: Rule: fermentation gives only 2 ATP per glucose but can be fast.
cards.quote: fermentation adds quick ATP and lactate builds up.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: A plant makes its own glucose by photosynthesis. Does it still need cellular respiration? Explain.
cards.back: Yes. Plant cells' jobs run on ATP, not glucose directly, so they break glucose down with oxygen to rebuild ATP. Photosynthesis builds the glucose; respiration releases its energy. Plants do both.
cards.quote: into carbon dioxide and water. Plants do both.
cards.section: Explain: with oxygen and without it

cards.front: A sealed jar holds a plant and a snail and is kept in total darkness. Can the jar keep running on its own? Why or why not?
cards.back: No. Atoms cycle between photosynthesis and respiration, but energy must arrive as light and leaves as heat. Without light, photosynthesis cannot rebuild glucose, so the cycle cannot keep running.
cards.why: Rule: atoms go round between the two processes; energy flows in as light and out as heat.
cards.quote: The atoms go round and round between them, while energy arrives as light and leaves as heat
cards.section: Explain: with oxygen and without it

cards.front: Why does the deep water of the Chesapeake Bay lose oxygen in summer?
cards.back: Algae die and sink; near the bottom, bacteria break them down by aerobic respiration, using up dissolved oxygen. The warm surface layer does not mix well with deep water, so little new oxygen arrives.
cards.quote: near the bottom bacteria break them down by aerobic respiration, using up the dissolved oxygen.
cards.section: Elaborate: the Bay’s summer oxygen gap

cards.front: Water with less than {{c1::2 milligrams of oxygen per liter (2 mg/L)}} is hypoxic.
cards.back: A large patch of it is often called a dead zone.
cards.quote: Water with less than 2 milligrams of oxygen per liter (2 mg/L) is hypoxic
cards.section: Elaborate: the Bay’s summer oxygen gap

cards.front: In summer, a strong storm mixes the Bay's warm surface water with the deep water. Predict the effect on oxygen at the bottom.
cards.back: Bottom oxygen should rise, because mixing brings new oxygen down to the deep water.
cards.why: Rule: bottom water loses oxygen in summer partly because the warm surface layer does not mix well, so little new oxygen reaches the bottom.
cards.quote: In summer the warm surface layer does not mix well with the deep water, so little new oxygen reaches the bottom.
cards.section: Elaborate: the Bay’s summer oxygen gap

cards.front: Model estimates of the Chesapeake Bay's largest one-day hypoxic volume were 9.8, 8.2, 10.7, 3.3, 9.8 and 10.1 km³ (2020 to 2025). Find the mean, rounded to the nearest whole number.
cards.back: Sum = 51.9 km³; 51.9 ÷ 6 = 8.65, which rounds to about 9 km³.
cards.quote: Find the mean of the six values, rounded to the nearest whole number.
cards.section: Elaborate: the Bay’s summer oxygen gap

cards.front: One year, rivers carry extra nutrients into the Bay. Use the respiration equation to predict what happens to the bottom water's oxygen.
cards.back: It should drop faster. More nutrients mean more algae, so more die and sink. Bacteria break them down by aerobic respiration, which uses oxygen (6O2 per glucose), so more food to break down uses up more oxygen.
cards.why: Rule: respiration consumes oxygen; algae growth is fed by nutrients from rivers.
cards.quote: Use the respiration equation: why would more sinking algae make the bottom water lose oxygen faster?
cards.section: Elaborate: the Bay’s summer oxygen gap

cards.front: Bottles of sugar water get live yeast, no yeast, or boiled yeast, each capped with a balloon. Only the live-yeast balloons inflate. What does this show, and what can it not tell you?
cards.back: The gas comes from live yeast breaking down sugar. But boiling kills the cells and also destroys their enzymes, so the test cannot say which of the two stopped the gas.
cards.quote: Boiling kills the cells and also destroys their enzymes, so this test cannot say which of the two stopped the gas.
cards.section: Design problem
